title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
kicker: How a library basement utility became the primary data governance layer for 400 million enterprise cloud seats.

epigraph.quote: In enterprise software, the most dangerous moment is not when your market is declining, but when your primary platform partner pivots underneath you. You either cannibalize your own perpetual cash cow to rebuild for the cloud, or you become a historical footnote.
epigraph.author: Dr. Tianyi (TJ) Jiang, Co-Founder and CEO, AvePoint (Investor Day Keynote)

web_blocks.html: AvePoint began in July 2001 in Somerset, New Jersey. It was founded by Dr. Tianyi Jiang and Kai Gong. They started in a public library basement with $3,000 in savings. Microsoft had just released SharePoint Portal Server 2001. Employees loved it for sharing files and project lists. But Microsoft's early architecture had a major flaw. If an employee deleted a document library, recovery was painful. The administrator had to restore the entire SQL database from tape. That took the whole server cluster offline for hours.

Dr. Jiang held a PhD in data mining from Rutgers University. He had built high-speed data systems at Lehman Brothers. He and Gong built DocAve. It was the first tool capable of granular, item-level SharePoint backup. Administrators could restore a single missing file in minutes. The product was an instant hit. For a decade, AvePoint rode the growth of on-premises SharePoint. DocAve expanded into migration, compliance, and archiving. The founders funded global growth entirely from cash flow. They took zero outside venture capital for their first thirteen years.

web_blocks.title: The Cannibalization Crossroads: The 2014 Office 365 Existential Crisis
paragraphs: In February 2014, Satya Nadella became Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft and famously declared that Microsoft was pivoting to a 'Mobile First, Cloud First' corporate mandate. Microsoft began aggressively migrating enterprise workloads from on-premises Exchange servers and local SharePoint deployments into Office 365 (later rebranded Microsoft 365).

For AvePoint, this platform pivot was an existential crisis. In 2014, over ninety percent of AvePoint's revenue came from high-margin, upfront perpetual software licenses and annual maintenance contracts for on-premises SharePoint. Under Nadella's cloud architecture, enterprise customers were abandoning local server infrastructure. If AvePoint clung to its perpetual licensing cash cow, its enterprise customer base would steadily evaporate. Jiang and Gong made the high-stakes decision to cannibalize their existing business: they froze new perpetual product lines, redirected hundreds of software developers, and spent four grueling years re-architecting their entire codebase into a multi-tenant, cloud-native Software-as-a-Service platform hosted directly on Microsoft Azure.

web_blocks.html: In 2014, Microsoft pivoted to the cloud under Satya Nadella. Enterprise workloads began shifting from on-premises servers into Office 365. This was an existential crisis for AvePoint. Over 90% of its revenue came from perpetual licenses for local servers. Jiang and Gong made a bold choice. They froze perpetual product development. They spent four years rebuilding their code into a cloud SaaS platform on Azure. Revenue growth slowed as upfront fees became ratable subscriptions. But by 2019, the cloud platform reached scale.

In December 2019, Sixth Street and Goldman Sachs led a $200 million growth investment. In July 2021, AvePoint went public on NASDAQ via Apex Technology Acquisition Corp. The deal raised $492 million in gross proceeds. The company was valued at $2.0 billion under ticker AVPT. In 2022, tech multiples compressed as interest rates rose. AVPT stock dropped over 70%, falling below $4 per share. But the business kept executing. ARR grew from $159 million in 2021 to $213 million in 2022. Gross margins held above 72%.

The public markets immediately tested management's mettle. As macroeconomic inflation surged and the Federal Reserve initiated aggressive interest rate hikes in early 2022, enterprise software multiples experienced a violent industry-wide compression. AvePoint's stock price de-rated by more than seventy percent from its post-merger peak above $15 to below $4 per share in late 2022, as institutional investors indiscriminately dumped SPAC-listed technology companies regardless of their underlying unit economics. Yet while market sentiment cratered, AvePoint's operational engine accelerated: annual recurring revenue (ARR) grew from $159 million in 2021 to $213 million in 2022, gross margins remained resilient above seventy-two percent. Management pivoted with ruthless discipline toward GAAP operating profitability.

Between 2023 and 2026, AvePoint proved its operating leverage. Management adhered to Rule of 40 discipline. ARR growth stayed above 26%, while non-GAAP operating margins reached 18.9%. In Q3 2026, total ARR hit $495.1 million, up 27% year over year. Net new ARR reached a record $30.0 million. Management raised full-year ARR guidance to $527 million. The company remains on track for $1.0 billion in ARR by 2029.

The early years taught the founders key operational lessons. They learned to run software engineering with zero financial debt. Every new developer hire was funded by customer cash flow. That early discipline shaped their long-term culture. It helped them weather the 2022 software market downturn with total calm.

AvePoint also expanded its international presence early. It opened technical centers across North America, Europe, and Asia. This global presence gave the firm 24/7 technical support capabilities. It also built strong relationships with international enterprise clients.

book_paragraphs: If you and I want to understand AvePoint, we cannot begin in the gleaming executive suites of Jersey City or the cloud data centers of Frankfurt and Tokyo. We have to walk back twenty-five years to the summer of 2001, into the basement of a public library in central New Jersey. Two young software engineers, Dr. Tianyi Jiang and Kai Gong, were staring at a CRT monitor displaying the early administrative console of Microsoft SharePoint Portal Server 2001. They were running on fumes, three thousand dollars in personal savings, and an intense technical obsession.

What did those two founders see that the rest of the software world missed? Microsoft had built a collaborative workspace that office workers loved because it let them share files, calendars, and project lists across local area networks without waiting for corporate IT. But Microsoft had engineered SharePoint with a massive structural vulnerability. In those early versions, content was pooled into monolithic SQL database tables. If an employee in marketing accidentally deleted an important departmental spreadsheet, there was no simple 'undo' button. The IT administrator had to restore the entire database from a tape backup, taking the whole company's collaborative network offline for half a day. Jiang and Gong asked a simple question: What if we could build a software surgical knife that reaches into the database, extracts that single lost document, and restores it in thirty seconds without anyone else noticing?

That utility was DocAve. It was unglamorous, highly technical, and completely indispensable. For thirteen years, AvePoint grew organically without taking a single penny of venture capital. Think about that discipline for a moment. In an industry where Silicon Valley founders routinely burned millions of dollars of other people's money to generate headline buzz, Jiang and Gong built AvePoint customer by customer, renewal by renewal. Every developer hire, every international office in Munich, Tokyo, and Singapore was paid for by cash collected from satisfied enterprise customers.

Then came February 2014, and with it, the most dangerous moment in AvePoint's history. Satya Nadella took the helm of Microsoft and issued his famous decree: Microsoft was going all-in on the cloud. The future was Office 365, and on-premises SharePoint servers were marked for extinction. Now put yourself in TJ Jiang's shoes. More than ninety percent of your revenue comes from selling high-priced perpetual software licenses and annual maintenance contracts for on-premises servers. Your sales reps are making fat commissions, your cash flow is predictable, and your customers are comfortable. But your primary platform host is shifting the ground beneath your feet.

Most software executives faced with that dilemma freeze. They protect their current quarter, harvest their legacy cash cow, and tell themselves that enterprise customers will never move their sensitive data to the public cloud. Jiang did the opposite. He recognized that if you do not cannibalize yourself, someone else will gladly do it for you. AvePoint froze development on its perpetual product lines and began the painful, expensive process of rewriting its entire code base into a multi-tenant cloud SaaS platform hosted on Microsoft Azure.

You and I must appreciate how difficult that transition really was. In SaaS, you do not collect a massive upfront license fee on day one; you collect modest monthly or annual installments while paying heavy Azure compute and storage bills upfront. Between 2015 and 2018, AvePoint's reported revenue growth slowed to a crawl. Competitors whispered that AvePoint was past its prime. But behind the scenes, the foundation for a modern compounding machine was being poured. By 2019, when enterprise cloud migrations hit exponential growth, AvePoint had the only enterprise-proven, multi-tenant governance and resilience platform ready to deploy at scale.

When AvePoint finally listed on the NASDAQ in July 2021 via a SPAC merger, raising nearly half a billion dollars, the timing looked brilliant. But then came the brutal tech crash of 2022. Wall Street indiscriminately hammered anything that had gone public via a SPAC. AvePoint's stock plunged by over seventy percent, trading below four dollars per share. An undisciplined management team would have panicked, laid off critical engineers, or chased low-quality revenue. AvePoint's founders, having survived on customer cash for their first thirteen years, simply lowered their heads and executed. They proved that software compounding is not about stock-market hype; it is about building software so deeply woven into enterprise IT operations that customers cannot turn it off even during a recession.

Consider the psychological fortitude that this multi-decade journey required. Many technology entrepreneurs build a company with the sole intention of selling it to Cisco, IBM, or Microsoft within five years. They optimize for a quick liquidity event, cash out, and walk away. Jiang and Gong took the harder path: they built AvePoint to last. When you listen to Dr. Jiang speak about data mining and enterprise architectures, you hear the voice not of a polished financial promoter. . But of an engineer who understands the plumbing of distributed databases down to the transistor level.

Notice also how AvePoint handled the geography of its software development. Rather than locating all its engineering talent in high-cost Silicon Valley where developer turnover averages eighteen months, AvePoint established deep, loyal engineering hubs in New Jersey, China, and Singapore. That global engineering footprint allowed AvePoint to maintain continuous 24/7 product development cycles while keeping research and development costs at a highly efficient ten to twelve percent of revenue. That structural cost advantage is something high-cost California rivals could never duplicate.

As we examine the company today. . It operates with ARR knocking on the door of half a billion dollars and GAAP operating profitability firmly established, remember this foundational lesson: AvePoint's moat was not born from venture capital subsidies. It was forged through twenty-five years of deep architectural symbiosis with Microsoft, tested by existential platform pivots, and governed by an ingrained culture of cash-flow discipline.

Reflect for a moment on the sheer operational grit required to manage an international software enterprise through three distinct corporate eras. When Dr. TJ Jiang and Kai Gong founded AvePoint in 2001, enterprise computing was dominated by local server closets and physical CD-ROM installations. They navigated the rise of enterprise virtualization, survived the 2008 global financial crisis by keeping overhead ruthlessly lean, and then voluntarily dismantled their perpetual licensing model to embrace multi-tenant cloud SaaS.

That ability to reinvent the business without destroying customer trust is the hallmark of enduring founder-led stewardship. In technology, companies that survive for a quarter-century are not those that chase every passing trend. . But those that anchor themselves to deep customer problems while adapting their delivery architecture to platform reality. That corporate resilience is an unquantifiable asset that cushions our investment against unforeseen industry shocks.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Asymmetric Advantage of Platform Symbiosis
book_callouts.text: Notice how AvePoint never tried to build its own standalone collaborative suite to compete with Microsoft. While hundreds of ambitious startups tried and failed to build 'the next SharePoint' or 'the next Slack,' AvePoint chose to be the indispensable tax collector on the world's dominant enterprise workspace. When you attach your software to an ecosystem that grows from ten million to four hundred million users, your primary job is simply not to get shaken off during platform transitions. By cannibalizing its perpetual licenses early, AvePoint earned another decade of compounding.
